reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / IDSA
clinicalPearls: Defined as pneumonia developing more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
Suspected when a ventilated patient develops new or progressive infiltrates with fever, leukocytosis, purulent secretions, and worsening oxygenation
Common pathogens include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), and other Gram-negative bacilli, with resistant organisms more likely in late-onset disease
Early-onset VAP tends to involve more antibiotic-susceptible organisms than late-onset VAP
Lower respiratory tract sampling for culture before starting antibiotics helps target and later de-escalate therapy
Management principles are prompt empiric antibiotics guided by local resistance patterns and patient risk factors, followed by de-escalation once cultures return
Risk factors for resistant organisms include recent antibiotic exposure, prolonged hospitalisation, and prior colonisation
Prevention bundles (head-of-bed elevation, sedation and ventilator weaning protocols, oral care, and subglottic secretion drainage) reduce incidence
reference.pathophysiology: The endotracheal tube bypasses upper airway defences and impairs the cough reflex and mucociliary clearance, while its surface accumulates a biofilm of microorganisms. Micro-aspiration of contaminated oropharyngeal and gastric secretions pooling above the cuff delivers pathogens to the lower airways. In critically ill patients the oropharynx becomes colonised with hospital flora, and impaired host defences allow these organisms to establish infection in the lung parenchyma, producing an inflammatory pneumonic process with impaired gas exchange.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary oedema from cardiac failure or fluid overload
infectionMimics: ARDS with new infiltrates but no infection
additionalInvestigations: Endotracheal aspirate or bronchoscopic sampling for Gram stain and quantitative or semiquantitative culture
Chest radiography or CT to assess infiltrates and complications
Arterial blood gases and oxygenation indices to gauge severity
Pleural fluid sampling if a significant effusion or empyema is suspected
redFlags: Progressive hypoxaemia and haemodynamic instability indicating severe pneumonia and possible septic shock requiring urgent escalation
Failure to improve on empiric therapy suggesting resistant organisms, complication, or wrong diagnosis
Development of empyema, lung abscess, or necrotising pneumonia
Multidrug-resistant pathogen risk warranting broader empiric cover
reference.prognosis: VAP prolongs mechanical ventilation and ICU stay and is associated with substantial attributable mortality, which is higher with resistant pathogens such as Pseudomonas, inappropriate initial antibiotics, and severe underlying illness; timely appropriate therapy improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Starting or continuing antibiotics for colonisation or non-infective infiltrates without adequate evidence of pneumonia
Choosing empiric therapy that ignores local resistance patterns and patient risk factors
Failing to de-escalate once culture results are available, promoting resistance
Overlooking preventable contributors and neglecting VAP prevention bundles
management: Start prompt empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics guided by local resistance patterns and onset timing, covering Pseudomonas aeruginosa and MRSA in late-onset or high-risk disease
Obtain lower respiratory tract samples for culture before antibiotics, then de-escalate to targeted therapy and limit the treatment course once results return
Provide supportive care with lung-protective mechanical ventilation, optimisation of oxygenation and management of accompanying sepsis
Apply a prevention bundle of head-of-bed elevation, daily sedation interruption with spontaneous breathing trials to enable early extubation, oral antiseptic care and subglottic secretion drainage
Achieve source control by draining an associated empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion
Monitor clinical response and reassess for resistant or alternative pathogens if the patient deteriorates or fails to improve
